sections.h2: Which selling route fits a house in St. Louis, MO?
sections.html:
Three routes exist for a St. Louis homeowner: hire a broker, go it alone, or hand the keys to an investor who pays cash for the property in its present condition. All three lead to the same city checkpoint, a Housing Conservation inspection that produces a Certificate of Inspection before the next household moves in.

Time is the real trade. Putting a house on the market invites the widest audience, yet you will clean, stage and sit through showings while a buyer's lender works through underwriting. An investor can often close on a date you pick, which helps when the house is vacant, inherited from a relative who lived elsewhere, or tied up with a tenant.

  • Broker listing: biggest pool of buyers, slowest clock, costs spelled out in the listing agreement.
  • Selling by owner: you price, show and negotiate, and a title company or attorney still has to close it.
  • Cash bid: few or no showings and a quicker closing, at a figure that accounts for repairs the buyer absorbs.

sections.h2: What kind of city is St. Louis for someone selling a home?
sections.html:
St. Louis is an independent city, which means it stands apart from St. Louis County. Wikipedia dates the split to 1877 and counts 79 officially recognized neighborhoods. That separation shapes a sale: the city ordinances, the city Recorder of Deeds and the city Collector of Revenue govern a house inside the limits, while a house across the boundary to the west falls under county and suburban rules.

Census estimates put the city at 278,144 residents in mid-2025, a drop of 7.7% from the April 2020 base. Only 45.3% of homes are lived in by their owners, so a large share of the stock is rented and many sellers are landlords or heirs. Brick defines the older housing: Laclede's Landing has cobblestone streets and brick and cast-iron warehouses, and many houses in Lafayette Square blend Greek Revival, Federal and Italianate styles.

Neighborhoods carry distinct identities. Dutchtown, Cherokee Street in Benton Park West and The Hill each have their own communities, and the Central West End sits beside the Washington University medical campus and the Cortex innovation district. Greater St. Louis is also home to seven Fortune 500 companies as of 2025, among them Centene, Emerson Electric and Edward Jones.

sections.h2: What happens with the occupancy inspection when a St. Louis house sells?
sections.html:
A sale of an occupied house triggers a new Certificate of Inspection when none has been issued in the prior 12 months. Building Division materials say 100% of the city lies inside a Housing Conservation District under Ordinance No. 71835, so the rule reaches every address in town.

The visit is a basic code check of interior and exterior conditions under the International Property Maintenance Code. The city says it is no guarantee or warranty of the building and suggests that purchasers consider a commercial grade inspection of their own. The practical details:

  • Fee: $120.00 to apply, or $200.00 if someone is found living in the dwelling without a current certificate.
  • Timing: the visit can be set for no sooner than 3 business days and no later than 15 days after the application.
  • Utilities: water and electric must be operating on inspection day.
  • Violations: when a certificate issues with violations, the owner gets 30 days to repair, and extensions can be granted for weather or other specific causes.
  • Validity: 12 months. The inspection also sets how many people may live in the unit, and no more than three unrelated persons may share a dwelling.

Apply online through the city permit portal or at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 425. The Building Division answers questions at (314) 622-3313.

sections.h2: How do St. Louis housing figures stack up?
sections.html:
Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a city with lower home values than the suburbs to its northwest. The middle owner-occupied value of $197,500 trails St. Charles at $298,700 and St. Peters at $269,900, though it is above St. Joseph at $154,200.

sections.h2: Where does a St. Louis deed get recorded?
sections.html:
Deeds for property in the city go to the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, in City Hall at 1200 Market Street, Room 126. Counter hours are weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., and the land records line is (314) 622-3260. A free online search of recorded land documents lets you confirm that your own deed, an old mortgage and any lien appear the way you expect before you sign a contract.

Missouri law lets spouses convey real estate by joint deed (RSMo 442.030). Where the property is held as an estate by the entirety, both spouses are bound by the covenants in the deed, so both sign. Heirs selling an inherited house should ask the title company which probate papers it needs to see.

On the tax side, ask the St. Louis Collector of Revenue what is currently owed on your parcel before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: How do storms and the ground affect a St. Louis house?
sections.html:
Summers run hot and sticky while winters turn cold. At Lambert airport the 1991 to 2020 normals show about 41.70 inches of precipitation and 16.6 inches of snow a year, and thunderstorms occur on roughly 48 days annually. Wikipedia adds that spring storms can bring high winds, large hail and tornadoes, and that the Great Flood of 1993 is part of the region's record.

Buyers and inspectors therefore look hard at roofs, gutters, chimneys and basements. The same article notes that the area south of downtown has numerous sinkholes and caves, though most caves in the city have been sealed. A cash buyer prices these conditions in directly, while a financed buyer may ask for repairs after a home inspection.

sections.h2: What should a St. Louis seller do first?
sections.html:
Begin with paperwork, then decide how much repair work is worth doing.

  • Pull your deed and payoff statements and compare them with the Recorder of Deeds online search.
  • Find out whether a Certificate of Inspection was issued in the last 12 months. If so, a new one may not be needed.
  • Walk the exterior for violations under the property maintenance code, since the city checks outside as well as inside.
  • Make sure water and electric will be on for inspection day.
  • Line up a listing estimate, a by-owner plan and a cash bid, and compare what you would actually keep from each.

If the house is vacant, damaged or occupied by a tenant, selling as-is for cash can remove several of these steps, although the buyer still needs the Certificate of Inspection before anyone occupies the unit.

faqs.q: Is an inspection required before a St. Louis house changes hands?
faqs.a: Yes, for an occupied house. The city requires a Certificate of Inspection when an occupied structure sells and none has been issued in the last 12 months. The application is $120.00, or $200.00 if the home is occupied without a current certificate.

faqs.q: How long does a St. Louis Certificate of Inspection last?
faqs.a: Twelve months. If violations are noted when it is issued, the owner has 30 days to correct them, with extensions possible for weather or other specific causes.

faqs.q: Does a house in poor shape have to be fixed before it sells in St. Louis?
faqs.a: Not always. The inspection is a basic code check and not a full condition report, and a cash buyer may take the house as it stands. The Certificate of Inspection is still required before anyone moves in.

faqs.q: Which office records the deed for a St. Louis sale?
faqs.a: The City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, City Hall Room 126, 1200 Market Street, phone (314) 622-3260. Your closing agent usually arranges the filing.

faqs.q: How many unrelated people can share a St. Louis dwelling?
faqs.a: No more than three. The Housing Conservation inspection also sets the number of people who may safely occupy the unit, which matters for rental properties being sold.
